variants.name: Sealed hierarchy of state types
variants.idiom_name: sealed state hierarchy with transitions returning the next state type (+ exhaustive when)
variants.implementation_notes: Kotlin's sealed hierarchies are the local idiom that replaces per-state protocol classes: each state is a subtype whose members are exactly its legal operations, transitions return the next state type, and when over the hierarchy is checked for exhaustiveness, so adding a state surfaces every dispatch that must handle it. The alternative realization keeps the phantom flavour - a generic PizzaBuilder<out S : BaseState> with extension functions declared only for one state type - which is preferable when one mutable-looking object must flow through a fluent API instead of being replaced by a new value at each step.
pitfalls: Sealed subclasses must live in the same module: a state added elsewhere breaks the closed-world assumption that exhaustiveness relies on.
Transitions that build a new state copy the payload; for large state data keep the shared, immutable part in one holder or use the phantom-type form.
Exhaustiveness only helps where the code narrows: a value entering from JSON or persistence arrives as the wide root type and re-introduces runtime checks.

variants.name: Phantom state parameter + constrained extension functions
variants.idiom_name: generic state parameter with extension functions declared per state
variants.implementation_notes: One class carries the state as a phantom type parameter (class PizzaBuilder<out S : BaseState>) and transitions are extension functions declared only for one instantiation, so the function exists exactly in that state. The parameter is never stored, so it costs nothing at run time; choose it when a fluent API must keep returning the same object rather than a new one, and accept the casts hidden in the transition bodies.
variants.code_sketch:
sealed interface BaseState
class CreamBase : BaseState
class TomatoBase : BaseState

class PizzaBuilder<out S : BaseState> private constructor()

fun PizzaBuilder<CreamBase>.withPotatoes() = PizzaBuilder<CreamBase>()
fun PizzaBuilder<TomatoBase>.withPineapple() = PizzaBuilder<TomatoBase>()
// PizzaBuilder<TomatoBase>().withPotatoes() does not compile
pitfalls: Type arguments are erased and the transitions cast internally, so a public constructor or an unchecked cast re-opens wrong-state calls.
Extension functions are resolved statically; forgetting the receiver constraint makes the transition available in every state.
